action_criteria.expected_evidence: Complete AV block with a wide LBBB-morphology escape at 32 bpm and left axis deviation; QTc 502 ms
action_criteria.label: Obtain a 12-lead ECG on arrival
action_criteria.rationale: The ECG is the first test in syncope; third-degree AV block on it is diagnostic of arrhythmic syncope and calls for immediate monitoring and pacing (ESC 2018).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Sodium 123 mEq/L and magnesium 1.6 mg/dL low on indapamide; potassium normal; creatinine 1.7 mg/dL
action_criteria.label: Electrolytes and renal function (BMP)
action_criteria.rationale: He takes a thiazide-like diuretic and has CKD: electrolytes exclude a reversible contributor to the block and reveal hyponatraemia that needs controlled correction (ESC 2018 targeted laboratory testing).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No intracranial haemorrhage or skull fracture; right parietal subgaleal swelling
action_criteria.label: Non-contrast head CT after the fall (age over 65, loss of consciousness, head strike)
action_criteria.rationale: He is 82, lost consciousness and struck his head: NICE NG232 indicates a head CT within 8 hours; it is a head-injury study, not part of the syncope diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Severe calcific aortic stenosis (AVA 0.8 cm2, mean gradient 46 mmHg, Vmax 4.4 m/s), concentric LVH, LVEF 46%
action_criteria.label: Transthoracic echocardiogram (restage the aortic stenosis)
action_criteria.rationale: Known aortic stenosis with a systolic murmur and syncope: echocardiography is Class I to grade the valve and LVEF, which decide valve intervention and the pacing system (ESC 2018; ESC/EACTS 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Persistent complete AV block with escape 29-43 bpm, presyncope at 30 bpm on walking, a 4.8 s pause; only brief non-sustained VT
action_criteria.label: Immediate in-hospital ECG monitoring (telemetry)
action_criteria.rationale: Syncope with complete AV block and severe aortic stenosis is high risk: immediate in-hospital monitoring is Class I until pacing and shows the escape stability and any ventricular arrhythmia (ESC 2018).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Basal septal enhancement beside the calcified annulus, concentric LVH, LVEF 46%
action_criteria.label: Cardiac MRI to characterise the myocardium (optional)
action_criteria.rationale: At 82 with calcific conduction disease and an established pacing indication, CMR does not change management; ESC 2021 pacing reserves it (IIa) for unexplained AV block under 60.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start AV-nodal blocking drugs (beta-blockers, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin) before pacing is secured
Do not correct the sodium by more than 10 mEq/L in the first 24 hours
Do not start or increase vasodilators in severe aortic stenosis
Do not discharge before a permanent pacemaker is implanted
required_recommendations: Recognise complete AV block from calcific degenerative conduction-system disease, with coexisting symptomatic severe aortic stenosis, as the cause of the syncope
Admit to a monitored bed with continuous ECG monitoring and transcutaneous pacing pads; temporary transvenous pacing if the escape becomes unstable before implantation
Implant a permanent dual-chamber pacemaker during this admission (ESC 2021 Class I for third-degree AV block), with latex-free precautions for his documented latex allergy
Refer to the Heart Team for aortic valve intervention, with TAVI favoured at 82 (ESC/EACTS 2025)
Stop indapamide and correct the sodium of 123 mEq/L slowly, limiting the rise to 10 mEq/L in the first 24 hours; replete magnesium
Hold telmisartan while blood pressure is low for him (106/55 mmHg) with severe aortic stenosis and hyponatraemia, and review antihypertensive therapy after the valve decision

Advise no driving until the pacemaker is implanted and the severe aortic stenosis has been treated: Group 1 drivers may resume 1 week after pacemaker implantation for the arrhythmic cause, and only once the structural cause is successfully treated (ESC 2018)

avoided_actions.rationale: No fever, meningism or encephalopathy: CSF has no role; the syncope is explained by complete AV block from calcific degenerative conduction disease with severe aortic stenosis.

Tilt testing is contraindicated in severe aortic stenosis and does not confirm cardiac syncope; the cause is complete AV block from calcific degenerative conduction disease with severe aortic stenosis.
Exercise testing is contraindicated in symptomatic severe aortic stenosis (ESC/EACTS 2025); the cause is complete AV block from calcific degenerative conduction disease with severe aortic stenosis.
EEG is not recommended in syncope (ESC 2018 Class III); there were no seizure features and the cause is complete AV block from calcific degenerative conduction disease with severe aortic stenosis.

Brain MRI is not indicated in syncope without focal signs (ESC 2018 Class III); the cause is complete AV block from calcific degenerative conduction disease with severe aortic stenosis, and the head injury is assessed by CT.

accepted: Cardiac syncope due to complete (third-degree) atrioventricular block secondary to calcific degenerative conduction-system disease

differential.key_features: Echo confirms severe stenosis (AVA 0.8 cm2, mean gradient 46 mmHg), which can cause syncope and needs intervention; telemetry documents complete AV block with presyncope at 30 bpm, and events also occurred seated.
LVH and QTc above 500 ms are a substrate, but telemetry shows only two 3-4 beat runs and the presyncope coincided with a rate of 30 bpm.
Two antihypertensives and hyponatraemia favour it, but episodes occurred seated and telemetry shows complete AV block during presyncope.
No chest pain or ST elevation; troponin I only mildly raised (0.06 ng/mL), in keeping with severe aortic stenosis, CKD and bradycardia.
No beta-blocker, non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker, digoxin or antiarrhythmic in the medication list.
Sudden loss of consciousness at 82 with ECG-documented complete AV block is not vasovagal.

general.query: syncope initial evaluation and risk stratification

results.key_finding: Initial evaluation comprises history, physical examination including supine and standing blood pressure, and a 12-lead ECG. High-risk features (syncope during exertion or supine, palpitations before the event, known structural or coronary disease, family history of sudden death under 40, high-risk ECG findings) call for early in-hospital evaluation with immediate ECG monitoring. Echocardiography is indicated when structural heart disease is known or suspected; EEG, brain imaging and routine laboratory panels are not recommended without a specific indication.
results.title: 2018 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope (Brignole M et al., Eur Heart J 2018;39:1883-1948)

results.key_finding: Risk stratification at the initial evaluation separates patients needing in-hospital monitoring and cardiac testing from those suitable for outpatient evaluation; targeted rather than routine blood testing is advised.
results.title: 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the evaluation and management of patients with syncope (Shen WK et al.)

general.summary: Guidelines base syncope work-up on the initial evaluation (history, examination, orthostatic BP, 12-lead ECG) and risk stratification; high-risk patients receive in-hospital ECG monitoring and targeted cardiac testing.

clinical_pearls: Calcific aortic stenosis is a common cause of acquired complete heart block in the elderly due to calcium extension from the aortic annulus into the adjacent His bundle and bundle branches
Cardiac syncope is characterized by sudden onset without prodrome and rapid full recovery without post-ictal confusion
Complete heart block is a Class I indication for permanent pacemaker implantation regardless of symptoms
Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis, syncope included, is a Class I indication for aortic valve intervention (ESC/EACTS 2025)
Prolonged QTc in the setting of bradycardia increases the risk of pause-dependent torsades de pointes

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Ryo Nakamura is an 82-year-old man with a significant cardiac history including moderate aortic stenosis, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and chronic kidney disease who presents to the emergency department via ambulance after his daughter found him unresponsive on the hallway floor of his apartment at approximately 6:45 AM. According to the patient and his daughter, he had gotten out of bed and was walking to the bathroom when he suddenly felt a brief sensation of the room going dark, followed immediately by loss of consciousness. He fell forward, striking the right side of his head on the wall. His daughter, who had arrived early to check on him, heard the thud and found him lying on the floor. She estimates he was unresponsive for approximately 15 to 20 seconds. She reports that she did not witness any shaking, jerking, or stiffening of the limbs. There was no foaming at the mouth, no tongue biting, and no urinary or fecal incontinence. Upon regaining consciousness, Mr. Nakamura was immediately lucid and coherent, asking his daughter why she was on the floor next to him. There was no period of confusion or disorientation. He reports a dull headache from striking the wall but denies any chest pain, shortness of breath, or palpitations before or after the event. Over the past two to three months, he has experienced four or five episodes of sudden lightheadedness lasting a few seconds each, sometimes accompanied by a sensation that his vision was graying out. These occurred at various times of day and in different positions, including while seated. He stopped his daily walks because of increasing fatigue and a fear of collapsing outside. He denies any prior seizures, and he has never had an episode of loss of consciousness before the recent cluster. He has not experienced any fever, weight loss, or night sweats. His daughter confirms he has been taking all his medications regularly; the only recent change was indapamide, added by his primary care physician four months ago for blood pressure.

neurological_exam.additional: No tongue laceration. No urinary incontinence. No evidence of prolonged convulsive activity. Right parietal scalp contusion from fall, no active bleeding. Systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur heard best at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids, consistent with known aortic stenosis.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose normal bilaterally, no dysmetria. Heel-to-shin normal bilaterally. No intention tremor. Rapid alternating movements intact.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: CN II: Visual fields full to confrontation bilaterally. Pupils equal, round, reactive to light 3mm to 2mm bilaterally. No papilledema on fundoscopic exam. Mild arteriolar narrowing noted bilaterally consistent with chronic hypertension. CN III/IV/VI: Extraocular movements intact, no nystagmus. CN V: Sensation intact to light touch in V1-V3 bilaterally. Masseter strength symmetric. CN VII: Face symmetric at rest and with activation. CN VIII: Hearing reduced bilaterally to finger rub without his hearing aids. CN IX/X: Palate elevates symmetrically. CN XI: Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius 5/5 bilaterally. CN XII: Tongue midline without fasciculations or atrophy.
neurological_exam.gait: Steady with normal base. Tandem gait intact. Romberg negative.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Glasgow Coma Scale 15. Speech is fluent with normal rate and volume. No dysarthria or aphasia. Attention intact — able to perform serial sevens to 72. Recall 3/3 objects at 5 minutes. No confusion, no post-ictal features at time of examination.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Tone normal, no rigidity or spasticity. Strength 5/5 in all major muscle groups of upper and lower extremities bilaterally. No pronator drift.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses are flexor (downgoing) bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch intact throughout. Pinprick mildly reduced in a stocking distribution below the ankles bilaterally, consistent with diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Vibration mildly diminished at bilateral great toes. Proprioception intact.
